use: Budget MIG welding on mild steel. Deep penetration, but lots of spatter (anti-spatter spray helps). The old-school standard before C25 became cheap.
THE most common MIG shielding gas for short-circuit work on steel: good penetration with little spatter. The default unless the procedure says otherwise.
Spray and pulsed-spray transfer on carbon steel, with a flatter, cleaner bead than C25. Stainless is usually run on a low-CO2 or argon-oxygen mix instead, to keep carbon out of the weld.
A spray-transfer mix: the small oxygen addition steadies the arc and helps the puddle wet out. Used for spray and pulsed-spray MIG on stainless and carbon steel. Not TriMix.
What "TriMix" usually means: mostly helium for a hotter, more fluid puddle, with a little CO2 for arc stability. Used for short-circuit MIG on stainless, where it keeps carbon pickup low.
The standard TIG gas, and the gas for aluminium MIG (CO2 and aluminium do not mix). Argon is heavier than air, so it blankets the puddle well.

proc: TIG aluminium + copper, MIG thick aluminium
use: Helium makes a hotter arc for thick aluminium and copper. Common mixes are 75/25, 50/50 and 25/75 argon/helium. Expensive, but needed on heavy aluminium.
A low-CO2 spray and pulsed-spray mix, common on stainless because so little CO2 adds very little carbon to the weld.
